doc.title: Germaine Bazzle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Teaching swing with movement and clapping on two and four
summary: She teaches the whole-body feel of swing, using 'Pick Yourself Up' and clapping on two and four; she is called a physical singer.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Why is that part of your teaching?

Because I want them to understand that music involves the entire being, you know. It’s not just a spiritual thing, it’s not just a physical thing. It’s all of you. I mean every part of your being works with this and to get them to understand the concept of swinging, of the swinging. It’s clapping, it’s patting your feet, that kind of thing. And when you’re singing, for me, I find that when I ask them to swing I’m asking you to dig in there and just let your soul be free and give me two and four. Just give me that swing on two and four you know. And it made a difference and the song that we were learning today, one of them, “Pick Yourself Up,” and we learned the lyrics and all. Then I said to them, “Clap while you sing it.” I said, “I want you to clap one, two, three, four, one.” So they sang it clapping one, two, three, four. Okay. Now clap it and sing and clap on one and three. One, three, one, three. I said now clap and sing on two and four. I said, “Now which one felt better?” They said, “Two and four.” I said that’s it. So to get them to understand that. It’s not rocket science, it’s just digging and dealing with what you have and being natural with it and being free to do that. And this is because I am told that I am a physical singer, and they’re right.
And physical in movement but also I think that must mean something beyond that you move around stage.

Yeah, right, yeah, yeah. It’s more than that, it’s more than that. But it’s almost to the point where I’m conducting you know, because the guys tell me, “I saw that shoulder moving.” I say, “You did, yeah.” So whatever the shoulder means, and I’m singing, whatever they get out of that shoulder, fine you know. If it’s going to bring us in and it’s going to make us tighter, fine. I don’t know what it means. They say, “Well when you’re singing you shake your leg” you know. I say, “Well I’m keeping time.” No there’s something else that’s happening when you do that. What am I communicating? I don’t know but whatever it is that they understand it to communicate, that’s it. But the whole thing, Monk, is it’s got to swing. It’s got to swing. And if I feel like I’m losing that then I know I am.
